pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Produce magnets using magnetic materials such as pieces of iron and a bar magnet, and using electricity.
- Demonstrate some applications of magnetic force in domestic and industrial activities, such as compasses, alarms and loudspeakers.
- Explore other industrial and domestic applications of magnetic force and present findings.

pages.title: What is a Magnet?
pages.body: A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field, giving it the ability to attract certain materials, particularly iron, nickel and cobalt, and to attract or repel other magnets. Magnets can occur naturally, but most magnets used in homes and industry are produced artificially using simple, reliable methods.

questions.q: A magnet is best described as an object that
o: Can only attract wood and plastic
Has no effect on iron, nickel or cobalt
Produces a magnetic field and can attract certain materials
questions.e: A magnet is an object that produces a magnetic field, giving it the ability to attract certain materials, particularly iron, nickel and cobalt, and to attract or repel other magnets.

pages.title: Simple Ways of Making Magnets
pages.body:
The stroking method and the electromagnet method are two simple, commonly demonstrated ways of making a magnet from ordinary iron materials.

- In the stroking method, a piece of unmagnetised iron, such as an iron bar or a needle, is stroked repeatedly in one direction using one pole of an existing bar magnet. This gradually aligns the tiny magnetic regions inside the iron in the same direction, turning it into a magnet.

- In the electromagnet method, an insulated copper wire is coiled tightly around an iron core, such as an iron nail, and connected to a battery (a source of direct current). As current flows through the coil, it creates a magnetic field that magnetises the iron core, producing an electromagnet that can be switched on and off simply by connecting or disconnecting the battery.

pages.title: Domestic and Industrial Applications of Magnetic Force
pages.body:
Compasses, cabinet catches, loudspeakers, alarms, scrapyard cranes, and electric motors are common domestic and industrial devices that rely on magnetic force, as summarised in the table below.

| **APPLICATION** | **HOW MAGNETIC FORCE IS USED** | **CATEGORY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Compass** | A small magnetised needle aligns itself with the earth's magnetic field to show direction | Domestic and navigational use |
| **Door and cabinet catches** | Small magnets hold doors or cabinet flaps firmly closed | Domestic use |
| **Loudspeakers** | A magnet interacts with an electric current in a coil to vibrate a cone and produce sound | Domestic and industrial use |
| **Electric bells and alarms** | An electromagnet attracts a metal striker to produce a ringing sound | Domestic and industrial use |
| **Cranes in scrapyards** | Powerful electromagnets lift and move large amounts of scrap metal | Industrial use |
| **Electric motors and generators** | Magnets interact with electric currents to produce or make use of motion | Industrial use |

Notice that magnetic force is used both in small, everyday domestic items, such as a compass or a cabinet catch, and in large scale industrial equipment, such as cranes that lift several tonnes of scrap metal using powerful electromagnets.

lessons.title: Methods of Making and Destroying Magnets in Detail

pages.title: Methods of Making and Destroying Magnets in Detail
pages.body:
| **METHOD** | **HOW IT IS DONE** | **RESULT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Single touch stroking** | Stroke a steel bar from one end to the other with one pole of a magnet. Lift the magnet high at the end of each stroke and repeat many times in the same direction | The end of the bar where each stroke finishes becomes the opposite pole to the stroking pole |
| **Double touch stroking** | Place the opposite poles of two magnets at the centre of the steel bar and stroke outwards to the two ends at the same time. Repeat many times | Each end of the bar becomes the opposite pole to the magnet that stroked it |
| **Electrical method** | Place the steel bar inside a coil of insulated wire called a solenoid and pass a direct current through the coil for a short time | The bar becomes a magnet. More turns of wire or a larger current give a stronger magnet |
| **Induction** | Bring an iron nail close to or in contact with a strong magnet | The nail becomes a temporary magnet and loses its magnetism when the magnet is removed |

Soft iron is easy to magnetise but loses its magnetism quickly, so it is used for temporary magnets and electromagnets. Steel is harder to magnetise but keeps its magnetism, so it is used for permanent magnets. A magnet is demagnetised by heating it strongly, by hammering it or by placing it in a coil that carries an alternating current.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:i6b730ce11|Fig 9.1  Two simple ways of making a magnet, the stroking method and the electromagnet method]]

Notice that the stroking method produces a permanent magnet that keeps its magnetism after the bar magnet is removed, while the electromagnet method produces a temporary magnet that loses most of its magnetism as soon as the electric current is switched off. This difference makes electromagnets especially useful in situations where a magnet needs to be turned on or off, such as in cranes used to lift and release scrap metal.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) machines used in hospitals are a further, more advanced application of magnetic force, using extremely strong magnets to help produce detailed images of the inside of the human body without the need for surgery. This shows that the same basic magnetic principles studied at this level, using magnets to attract, repel or interact with electric currents, extend all the way from simple classroom demonstrations to advanced medical technology.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**

pages.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
pages.body: Newton's Second Law of motion states that the acceleration of an object depends on the force applied to it and on the mass of the object, and can be written as force equals mass multiplied by acceleration. This means that for a fixed force, a smaller mass will accelerate more, while a larger mass will accelerate less. Similarly, for a fixed mass, a larger force will produce more acceleration, while a smaller force will produce less.

lessons.title: Newton's Second Law in Daily Life

pages.title: Newton's Second Law in Daily Life
pages.body:
Pushing objects of different masses, kicking balls of different weights, and lifting objects with magnetic force are everyday situations that clearly demonstrate Newton's Second Law of motion, as summarised in the table below.

| **EXAMPLE** | **FORCE INVOLVED** | **EFFECT ON MOTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Pushing an empty wheelbarrow** | A moderate push force on a small mass | Produces a large acceleration, so it speeds up quickly |
| **Pushing a fully loaded wheelbarrow** | The same push force on a much larger mass | Produces a small acceleration, so it speeds up slowly |
| **Kicking a light football** | A kick force on a small mass | Produces a large acceleration, so the ball moves off quickly |
| **Kicking a heavy medicine ball** | The same kick force on a larger mass | Produces a small acceleration, so the ball moves off slowly |
| **An electromagnet lifting a small nail** | A magnetic force acting on a small mass | Produces a large acceleration, lifting the nail quickly |
| **An electromagnet lifting a large iron block** | The same magnetic force acting on a larger mass | Produces a small acceleration, lifting the block slowly |

pages.title: The Relationship Between Magnetic Force and Newton's Second Law
pages.body: Magnetic force is one particular type of force, and like any other force, it obeys Newton's Second Law of motion when it acts on an object. When an electromagnet exerts a magnetic force on a small iron nail, the nail experiences a large acceleration and moves towards the magnet quickly, since it has a small mass. When the same electromagnet exerts a similar magnetic force on a much larger iron object, the object experiences a smaller acceleration and moves more slowly, since it has a larger mass. This shows that Newton's Second Law applies to magnetic force in exactly the same way it applies to a push, a pull, or any other type of force.

pages.title: A Simple Experiment Using Magnetic Force
pages.body:
Setting up an electromagnet, testing it on a light object, then testing it on a heavier object, and comparing the results are the four general steps of a simple experiment that can demonstrate the relationship between magnetic force and Newton's Second Law of motion.

- First, construct or obtain an electromagnet, similar to the one described in Lesson 9, connected to a battery.

- Second, place a small, light iron object, such as a paperclip, near the electromagnet, switch on the current, and observe how quickly it accelerates towards the magnet.

- Third, replace the paperclip with a larger, heavier iron object of a similar shape, and repeat the same test using the same electromagnet and the same distance.

- Fourth, compare how quickly each object accelerated towards the magnet, and relate the difference in acceleration to the difference in mass, in line with Newton's Second Law of motion.

pages.title: Units and Worked Examples on Newton's Second Law
pages.body:
Newton's second law is written as force = mass x acceleration, or F = m x a. Force is measured in newtons, written N. Mass is measured in kilograms, written kg. Acceleration is measured in metres per second squared, written m/s². One newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s². The formula can be rearranged to find the acceleration, which is force divided by mass, or the mass, which is force divided by acceleration.

| **QUESTION** | **WORKING** | **ANSWER** |
|---|---|---|
| **A trolley of mass 2 kg accelerates at 3 m/s². Find the force on it** | Force = mass x acceleration = 2 x 3 | 6 N |
| **A force of 20 N acts on a box of mass 4 kg. Find its acceleration** | Acceleration = force divided by mass = 20 divided by 4 | 5 m/s² |
| **A force of 30 N gives a cart an acceleration of 6 m/s². Find the mass of the cart** | Mass = force divided by acceleration = 30 divided by 6 | 5 kg |
| **The same force of 12 N is applied to a 2 kg ball and to a 6 kg ball. Compare their accelerations** | 12 divided by 2 = 6 and 12 divided by 6 = 2 | The 2 kg ball accelerates at 6 m/s² and the 6 kg ball at 2 m/s², so the lighter ball speeds up three times as fast |

The examples show the two ideas in the law. For the same mass, a larger force gives a larger acceleration. For the same force, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration.

Newton's Second Law also helps explain why heavier vehicles, such as loaded trucks, generally accelerate more slowly than lighter vehicles, such as cars, when their engines produce a similar amount of force. Engineers take this relationship into account when designing vehicles, machinery and even safety features, since understanding how mass affects acceleration for a given force is essential for predicting how objects will move in real world situations.

pages.title: Recap, What is a Simple Machine?
pages.body: A simple machine is a basic device that changes the size or direction of a force to make work easier, using few or no moving parts. The lever, the wheel and axle, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, and the screw are the six basic types of simple machines studied previously in Basic 7. Each simple machine works alone to make a specific task, such as lifting, cutting or moving an object, easier than it would be without it.

questions.e: A simple machine is a basic device that changes the size or direction of a force to make work easier, using few or no moving parts.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the six basic types of simple machines?
questions.e: The lever, the wheel and axle, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, and the screw are the six basic types of simple machines studied previously in Basic 7.

pages.title: What is a Complex Machine?
pages.body: A complex machine is a device made up of two or more simple machines working together to perform a task that a single simple machine could not easily achieve on its own. While a simple machine, such as a single lever, can only perform one basic action, a complex machine combines several of these basic actions to carry out more advanced, multi step tasks, such as transporting a person over long distances or grinding large quantities of grain.

pages.title: Identifying Simple Machines Within Complex Machines
pages.body:
Bicycles, wheelbarrows, cars, sewing machines and grain milling machines are common complex machines that can each be broken down into the individual simple machines they contain, as summarised in the table below.

| **COMPLEX MACHINE** | **SIMPLE MACHINES IT CONTAINS** | **HOW IT IMPROVES QUALITY OF LIFE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Bicycle** | Wheel and axle, lever (handlebar and pedals), and screws | Provides an efficient, low cost way to travel and transport small loads |
| **Wheelbarrow** | Wheel and axle, and lever | Makes it easier to move heavy loads such as soil, sand or produce |
| **Car** | Wheel and axle, screws, and inclined planes (in some components) | Allows fast, comfortable travel over long distances |
| **Sewing machine** | Wheel and axle, lever, and screw | Allows faster, more precise stitching of clothing and other materials |
| **Grain milling machine** | Wheel and axle, and wedge (grinding surfaces) | Processes large quantities of grain quickly, saving time and effort |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How Complex Machines Improve Quality of Life

pages.title: How Complex Machines Improve Quality of Life
pages.body: Saving time, reducing physical effort, increasing precision, and enabling entirely new activities are four important ways complex machines improve quality of life. A bicycle allows a person to travel much further in a day than walking would allow, using considerably less physical effort per unit distance. A sewing machine allows clothing to be produced more quickly and with more precise, even stitching than sewing by hand. A grain milling machine can process in minutes an amount of grain that would take many hours to grind by hand. In each case, the complex machine takes on part of the physical burden of a task, freeing up time and energy for other activities.

pages.title: Look at the picture
pages.body:
[[img:if96e64531|Fig 11.1  A bicycle as an example of a complex machine, made up of several simple machines working together]]

Notice how the wheels and axles allow the bicycle to roll smoothly, the pedals and handlebar act as levers to apply and direct force, and the screws hold the frame and components firmly together. On its own, none of these simple machines could transport a person efficiently, but combined together in the right arrangement, they form a highly effective complex machine.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Many modern complex machines, such as cars and industrial equipment, also include electrical and electronic components, such as motors, sensors and circuit boards, alongside their mechanical simple machines. This shows that the idea of a complex machine has expanded over time to include not just combinations of simple mechanical machines, but also combinations of mechanical and electronic systems working together to perform even more advanced tasks.

A complex machine combines multiple simple machines to perform advanced tasks
A complex machine has no relationship to simple machines
A simple machine always contains more parts than a complex machine

questions.q: A complex machine is best described as
o: A device made of two or more simple machines working together
A single simple machine used alone
A tool with absolutely no moving parts
A type of natural energy source
questions.e: A complex machine is a device made up of two or more simple machines working together to perform a task that a single simple machine could not easily achieve on its own.

questions.q: Complex machines improve quality of life mainly by
o: Increasing physical effort required for tasks
Making all tasks impossible to complete
Reducing time and effort needed to complete tasks
Removing the need for any machines at all
questions.e: How Complex Machines Improve Quality of Life Saving time, reducing physical effort, increasing precision, and enabling entirely new activities are four important ways complex machines improve quality of life.

o: Removing the need for thread completely
Requiring more physical effort than hand sewing

questions.q: Modern complex machines increasingly combine simple machines with
questions.e: Many modern complex machines, such as cars and industrial equipment, also include electrical and electronic components, such as motors, sensors and circuit boards, alongside their mechanical simple machines.
